Chapter 8: Applying the Framework — Games in Work, Family, and Social Life.
You know, the ideas behind ego states, transactions, and games aren’t just something you spot in close relationships. They’re everywhere—at work, around the dinner table, even when you’re just hanging out with friends.
The real power comes when you start to notice these patterns in all areas of your life. Spotting and shifting these games can totally transform how you connect, collaborate, and communicate.
Let’s start with the workplace. This is a place where games often revolve around things like power, recognition, and who’s responsible for what. Ever seen the “Now I’ve Got You” game? It’s that moment when someone’s just waiting for a mistake—ready to pounce and assign blame. Or the “If It Weren’t For You” game, where somebody’s always frustrated but never really takes action to change things. These patterns can drag down morale and create a culture of tension.
So how do you break the cycle? First, encourage adult-to-adult conversations. Set the expectation that everyone speaks directly and respectfully. If you notice a game starting, don’t let it linger. Call it out gently and invite a new way of handling things. And if you’re in a leadership role, modeling vulnerability makes a huge difference. When leaders admit mistakes and ask for feedback, it sets a tone of authenticity that everyone can feel.
Now, let’s talk about families. Family games often get baked into our routines and even passed down through generations. Think about patterns like “See What You Made Me Do” or “Why Don’t You—Yes But.” These games trap people in cycles of blame and helplessness.
Breaking free starts with setting clear boundaries—making it obvious what’s okay and what’s not in family conversations. Encourage everyone to share how they feel and what they need, without anyone jumping to judgment. And when you spot a familiar game creeping in, don’t be afraid to gently point it out and suggest a different route. Sometimes that’s all it takes to shift the script.
What about social settings? Games here can be a little sneakier, but they still have an impact. Maybe there’s a friend who always plays the “Martyr,” putting everyone’s needs ahead of their own and then quietly feeling resentful afterward. These moments are a chance for awareness and gentle honesty. Sometimes, just naming what’s happening can help the group move in a better direction.
No matter where you are—at work, with family, or among friends—the heart of the matter is this: When you recognize the game, try to understand the deeper need behind it. Then, choose a response that respects both your needs and the needs of others.
That’s how you build healthier, more genuine connections in every part of your life.
